name: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
title: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
answer: Testing a study design before data collection means checking whether a planned quantitative study can answer its research question before resources are spent gathering real data. It covers sample size and power calculations, simulation of the proposed analysis under plausible effect sizes, and pilot runs with synthetic or existing data. The goal is to catch weak designs, measurement problems, and analysis mismatches early. This practice sits within reproducible quantitative work because a design that is tested in advance is easier to document and rerun later.

sections.body: Testing a study design before data collection means checking whether a planned quantitative study can answer its research question before resources are spent gathering real data. It covers sample size and power calculations, simulation of the proposed analysis under plausible effect sizes, and pilot runs with synthetic or existing data. The goal is to catch weak designs, measurement problems, and analysis mismatches early. This practice sits within reproducible quantitative work because a design that is tested in advance is easier to document and rerun later.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work usually runs on a standard statistical computing environment such as R or Python with packages for simulation and power analysis. A laptop or a small cloud instance is often enough, since the datasets are synthetic or small pilot extracts rather than full production data. Version control and a scripted pipeline let the same design test be rerun when assumptions change. No specialised hardware is required for most design testing.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is to write a small simulation that generates data from a model of the expected effect, then run the planned analysis on many simulated datasets and record how often the result is detected or estimated well. Power analysis sets the sample size needed for a given effect and acceptable error rates. Pilot testing with a few real or synthetic cases checks that measures load, code runs, and the analysis plan produces interpretable output. Pre-registration of the tested design then locks the plan before real data collection begins.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk here are mostly about transparency and misuse of preliminary results. A design test uses assumptions that may be wrong, so its outputs are planning aids, not findings about the real world. Researchers should document the simulation code, the assumed effect sizes, and the decision rules so others can audit the design. There is a risk of p-hacking or design shopping if many variations are tried and only the one that looks best is reported, so the tested plan should be fixed before data collection. Provenance of any pilot data must be clear, especially if existing data are reused.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Design testing is moving toward more automated simulation and synthetic data generation, so a researcher can stress-test a plan against many plausible data-generating processes at once. Closer links with pre-registration platforms and reproducible workflow tools are making the tested design a standard part of the research record. As quantitative work grows more complex, testing the design before data collection is likely to become a routine step rather than an optional check.
